terms.definition: The direct cost of inventory or materials sold to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: COGS affects gross profit and pricing decisions.

terms.definition: Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity — the identity every transaction must leave intact, which is why a single-sided entry is always an error.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting Applications items give two of the three figures and ask for the third, and the same identity is what a competitor uses to prove a balance sheet balances.

terms.definition: A system recording every transaction in at least two accounts so that total debits equal total credits, which is what makes an out-of-balance ledger detectable.
terms.whyItMatters: An ACT roleplay asking a competitor to explain why the books will not balance expects this rule, not a search for a missing receipt.

terms.definition: The left side of an account, which increases assets and expenses but decreases liabilities, equity and revenue — direction depends on the account type, not on whether money came in.
terms.whyItMatters: Journalizing items on the accounting exam are lost by assuming a debit always means an increase, which is only true for half the account types.

terms.definition: The right side of an account, which increases liabilities, equity and revenue but decreases assets and expenses — the mirror of a debit, and unrelated to a credit card.
terms.whyItMatters: Recording a cash sale on the exam requires debiting cash and crediting revenue; reversing the pair is the single most common journalizing error.

terms.definition: A two-column sketch of one account with debits on the left and credits on the right, used to work out an entry before it is journalized.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors use these to reason through a multi-account transaction under exam time pressure rather than journalizing straight from memory.

terms.definition: A period-end entry recording revenue earned or expense incurred that no cash transaction has yet captured, such as accrued wages or expired prepaid insurance.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask what happens if one is skipped: the statements misstate both net income and the balance sheet for that period.

terms.definition: A period-end entry zeroing revenue, expense and drawing accounts into equity so the next period starts fresh, while asset and liability balances carry forward.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing which accounts close from which carry over is a recurring accounting-exam item and the reason temporary and permanent accounts are named that way.

terms.definition: Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped produce, not in the period they were paid, which is what forces period-end adjustments.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the reason an ACT scenario records December commissions against December sales even though the checks clear in January.

terms.definition: Revenue is recorded when the good or service is delivered, not when the order is signed or the cash arrives, so a deposit on undelivered work is a liability.
terms.whyItMatters: A client in an accounting roleplay who wants to book a prepayment as this month's sales is asking for something this rule forbids.

terms.definition: Financial statements are prepared on the premise the business will keep operating, which is why assets are carried at cost rather than at what they would fetch in a liquidation.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains an exam answer competitors find odd — that a balance sheet does not report what a company is worth if sold today.

terms.definition: Cost minus salvage value divided by useful life, producing the same expense every year of an asset's life.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting exam items hand over a purchase price, a salvage value and a life expectancy and expect the annual figure computed, not estimated.

terms.definition: An accelerated method applying a fixed rate to the asset's remaining book value, so expense is largest in year one and falls every year after.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing between this and the straight-line method changes reported net income early in an asset's life, which is exactly what an exam item tests.

terms.definition: An inventory costing method assuming the oldest units sell first, which in a period of rising prices leaves newer, costlier units on the balance sheet and reports higher profit.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting items give a purchase history and ask for ending inventory; the costing method chosen changes the answer even though the physical goods are identical.

terms.definition: An inventory costing method assuming the newest units sell first, which under rising prices charges the higher costs against revenue and reports lower profit and lower tax.
terms.whyItMatters: The tax consequence is the point of the exam item: two firms with identical inventory report different net income purely on this choice.

terms.definition: Costing inventory at total cost of goods available divided by total units available, so every unit carries the same average cost regardless of when it was bought.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the third answer choice on every inventory-costing item, and it lands between the FIFO and LIFO figures under rising prices.

terms.definition: Recording revenue and expenses only when cash moves, which is simpler than the accrual basis but reports a month's profit in whichever period the payment happens to land.
terms.whyItMatters: An ACT roleplay advising a small client on which basis to use rests on this distortion, and most businesses above a size threshold may not use it.

terms.definition: An account deliberately carrying a balance opposite its partner — accumulated depreciation against an asset, sales returns against revenue — so the original figure stays visible alongside the reduction.
terms.whyItMatters: It answers the exam item asking why equipment still shows its full purchase price years after it was bought.

terms.definition: A contra-asset estimate of receivables that will never be collected, recorded in the period of the sale rather than when a specific customer's account is finally written off.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting items test the timing: estimating bad debt up front is what keeps the expense in the same period as the revenue it came from.

terms.definition: The common rule set governing how U.S. financial statements are prepared, which is what lets an outside reader compare two companies' books at all.
terms.whyItMatters: An ACT roleplay where a client wants to record something a convenient way is answered by whether these rules permit it, not by whether it looks reasonable.

terms.definition: Cash collected before the work is delivered, recorded as a liability rather than income until the obligation is filled.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounting items give a customer deposit and ask where it lands on the statements; calling it revenue overstates income for the period.

terms.definition: Cash paid ahead for a future benefit — insurance or rent — carried as an asset and expensed a period at a time as it is used up.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the standard period-end adjustment on the accounting exam: the payment happened once, the expense belongs to several months.

terms.definition: An asset's original cost minus accumulated depreciation, which is what the ledger reports and rarely what the asset would sell for.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask for the reported value of equipment after three years, and the answer requires subtracting the accumulated total, not one year's depreciation.

terms.definition: Net credit sales divided by average receivables, counting how many times a year a business collects what customers owe it.
terms.whyItMatters: A falling figure in an accounting scenario is the early warning that credit customers are paying slower, before any account goes bad.

terms.definition: Updating inventory and cost of goods sold at every sale, so the balance is known continuously — unlike a periodic system, which learns it only from a physical count.
terms.whyItMatters: Which system a business runs decides whether an ACT scenario can state cost of goods sold mid-period or has to wait for the count.

terms.definition: The procedures protecting assets and records — separating who authorizes, who records and who holds the cash — so no one person can both commit and conceal an error.
terms.whyItMatters: An ACT roleplay asking how a small business prevents theft expects this separation of duties, not stricter hiring.
